column1: # core/spec/divergent.tsv — the core-level parity debt, one row per divergence.
# One row per expression, tab-separated:  expr <TAB> go <TAB> ts <TAB> note
# Same comment and escaping rules as the other core/spec files, and the same
# two-runner discipline: core/go/corespec_test.go asserts the `go` column and
# core/ts/src/corespec.test.ts asserts the `ts` column, so both suites stay
# green while the difference stays PINNED. If either engine moves, its column
# fails and the row is re-examined rather than silently re-baselined. Each
# runner also FAILS a row whose go and ts columns are EQUAL — a fixed
# divergence must MOVE to the spec file it belongs in, or this stops being an
# honest debt list.
# SHRINK-ONLY, exactly as parser/spec/divergent.tsv is.
# WHERE THESE CAME FROM. The 1808-row engine crossdiff has been green
# throughout, and so has every core/spec row. None of these were visible to
# either, because a differential that hard-fails only when both engines
# SUCCEED with different values cannot see two engines that both fail, and
# because no source in eng/spec builds the shapes below. They were found by
# sweeping core/ts's UNCOVERED regions — the parser half of this program
# established that an uncovered branch in one port is where a divergence
# hides, and this file is that finding applied to core.
# The `go` column is the reference by CONVENTION, not by proof. Two of the
# five original parser-side divergence classes turned out to have Go wrong.
# Read design/CORE-TS-DIVERGENCES.1.md before assuming which side moves.
run [q ( ) ]
column4: DATA: TS drops an empty paren group and re-associates operands; Go raises no_value_error.

column1: # --- a type-mismatched paren operand: which error ---------------------------
# Both refuse; they disagree about the code. Go reports signature_error (the
# operand does not fit the slot); core/ts reports no_value_error (it treats
# the group as having produced nothing usable). Same refusal, different
# taxonomy, so a caller matching on the code behaves differently.
run boomq end
column4: DATA: TS resolves the WORD `end` to the end marker; core/go has no such word and raises undefined_word.

column1: run 1 boomq end
column4: DATA: TS resolves the WORD `end` to the end marker; core/go has no such word and raises undefined_word.

column1: # --- the builtin type-name table, and slash paths ---------------------------
# core/ts's leaf name table is narrower than core/go's and has no path form.
# `Word` is worse than a miss: core/ts CRASHES with an uncoded error
# (`AsWord: not a word value`), which is a non_boru failure escaping the
# taxonomy entirely — the one row here that is a defect on any reading.
run Word/__ED
column4: DATA: TS now RESOLVES the path, but canons the End type LITERAL through the End marker arm and renders nothing; Go renders the leaf __ED. The same vType/payload conflation isWord() had, one arm over.

column1: run [ Module ]
column4: DATA: core/ts type-name table is narrower; `Word` escapes the error taxonomy entirely.

column1: # --- canon of a bare paren marker: ADJUDICATED, and TS is right -------------
# Go renders an OpenParen as the EMPTY string, so a list holding one renders
# with a gap and the token vanishes; core/ts renders `(`.
# The `go` column is NOT the reference here, and Go's own source says so.
# core/go/canon.go:104 fixed exactly this defect for the CLOSE paren — "Canon
# had no arm, so the payload-less fallthrough rendered it as the empty string
# and `1 )` canon'd to `1 `, dropping the token silently" — and the same
# commit fixed it for the End marker. The OPEN paren was left because, as the
# comment says, "an unmatched OPENING paren never reaches here, because that
# is a parse error rather than a value". The corpus notation can construct one
# where the parser cannot, and the fallthrough is still there.
# So these rows stay pinned with core/ts UNCHANGED. Making TS reproduce Go's
# fallthrough would be applying a known defect to the port. The ledger header
# warns that the go column is the reference "by convention, not by proof";
# this is the third time on this programme that the warning has paid.
list (

column1: # --- an unquoted EVAL-LIST def binding: data or code? --------------------
# Go SUBSTITUTES the list as a value, which then auto-evaluates — `[3]`.
# core/ts SPLICES it as a code body and runs it in place — `3`. The quoted
# spelling agrees on both (`[q …]` is opaque data), so the disagreement is
# exactly about what an UNQUOTED list binding means.
# Found the moment the corpus could install a def at all, which is the
# point: this surface had no rows, so nothing had ever compared the two
# engines on it. core/ts/src/engine.test.ts BASELINES the TS answer in
# "splices an unquoted eval list as a code body" — the second time on this
# branch that a per-engine unit test has pinned one engine's behaviour as
# the contract.
run def b [ addq 1 2 ] ; b
column4: DATA: Go substitutes the list as a value; TS splices it as a code body.

column1: run def b [ 1 2 ] ; b
column4: DATA: same rule with no words in the body — the residual is the list, not its elements.

column1: # --- the UNIFIER's type-constructor surface ---------------------------------
# Opened on 2026-08-09 by `unifyq` plus the d( ) / [: ] / {: } notation
# (core/spec/unify.tsv explains both). Until then no corpus row reached
# unification at all, so this whole class was invisible to an instrument
# built to compare the two ports — the sharpest instance yet of the rule
# that an uncovered surface is where a divergence hides.
# ONE cause under most of it: core/go's `Unify` dispatches on Shape() into
# per-family handlers (unify_disjunct.go, unify_list.go, unify_map.go, …),
# while core/ts's `unifiesValue` is a flat 40-line function with arms for
# lists, maps and scalars and NOTHING for a disjunct or a typed container.
# What disjunct logic core/ts has lives in isValueOfType, which the
# symmetric unifier never calls.
# The typed-MAP rows are worse than a wrong answer: core/ts throws a raw
# `AsMap: not a map value`, an uncoded JS error escaping as a non-boru
# failure. That one is a defect to fix, not debt to hold, and it is first
# in the queue.
# NOT ledgered as permanent: this is a PORT gap with a known shape, and
# the rows are here to make the fix visible when it lands. The 82 rows in
# unify.tsv are the part that already holds.
run unifyq 5 d( Integer String )
column4: DATA: core/ts unifiesValue has NO disjunct arm — the disjunct logic lives only in isValueOfType, not in the symmetric unifier.
